Specification: **Arg1** — *the converse of a statement; the contrapositive of a statement; the
relationship between the truth of a statement and its converse and its contrapositive.*
Official source: **Notes on Logic and Proof**, pp. 43–49.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why learn this when TMUA is multiple choice?

You never write a proof on TMUA — every question is **multiple choice**. But the exam tests whether you
can **judge** a claim: which of these is the contrapositive? does the converse follow? Being able to swap
and negate an "if … then …" correctly in your head is exactly what lets you pick the right option in
seconds.
:::

<div class="fs-sub">From one statement "if P then Q" you can build three relatives. The one rule that matters: the <strong>contrapositive is always equivalent</strong> to the original; the <strong>converse almost never is</strong>.</div>

## The original and its three relatives

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Build them from "if $P$ then $Q$"

Start from $P\Rightarrow Q$.

$$\textbf{Converse:}\ \text{if } Q \text{ then } P \quad(\text{swap})$$
$$\textbf{Inverse:}\ \text{if not }P\text{ then not }Q \quad(\text{negate both})$$
$$\textbf{Contrapositive:}\ \text{if not }Q\text{ then not }P \quad(\text{swap }\textbf{and}\text{ negate})$$
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Contrapositive — **always** equivalent

$$\text{"if }P\text{ then }Q\text{"}\ \equiv\ \text{"if not }Q\text{ then not }P\text{"}$$

Same truth value, every time. This is why **proof by contrapositive** is valid: to prove $P\Rightarrow Q$
you may instead prove $\text{not }Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$.

[to prove "if $n^2$ even then $n$ even", prove the contrapositive "if $n$ odd then $n^2$ odd"]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Converse — almost **never** equivalent

The converse is a **separate** statement, with its own truth value. A true statement can have a false
converse.

[$x>3\Rightarrow x>0$ is true, but its converse $x>0\Rightarrow x>3$ is false ($x=1$)]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The equivalence map

| This form | has the same truth value as |
|---|---|
| **original** | **contrapositive** |
| **converse** | **inverse** |

[original & contrapositive stand or fall together; converse & inverse stand or fall together]{.eg}
:::

::::

## In practice, and the trap

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Form each one fast

**Converse:** swap the two halves. **Inverse:** negate both halves (keep order). **Contrapositive:**
do both — swap *and* negate.

Only the **contrapositive** is guaranteed to match the original.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The trap — assuming the converse

"If $P$ then $Q$" does **not** give you "if $Q$ then $P$." Treating a statement and its converse as the
same thing is the classic Arg1 error — and if both happen to hold, that is exactly an **if and only if**.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Link to necessary / sufficient

$P\Rightarrow Q$ says $P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$ and $Q$ is **necessary** for $P$. The **converse**
$Q\Rightarrow P$ swaps those roles — which is why it is a genuinely different claim.
:::

::::

:::::

## Notes

From $P \Rightarrow Q$ you may deduce one thing for free, and one thing not at all. There are **three** ways
to rearrange an implication, and only **one** of them says the same thing as the original. Mixing them up is
the most expensive mistake in Paper 2, because every *"which of these is equivalent?"* question turns on it.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Two words that are easy to swap.** It is the **contrapositive** that is always equivalent to the original.
The **converse** almost never is. A one-second check: **the contrapositive has negations in it; the converse
does not.**
:::

### The three relatives of "if $P$ then $Q$"

| Name | Form | Built by | Equivalent to the original? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Original** | if $P$ then $Q$ | — | — |
| **Converse** | if $Q$ then $P$ | swap | **No** |
| **Inverse** | if not $P$ then not $Q$ | negate both | **No** |
| **Contrapositive** | if not $Q$ then not $P$ | swap **and** negate | **Yes, always** |

Take "if $n$ is divisible by $6$, then $n$ is even", which is true.

- **Converse:** if $n$ is even, then $n$ is divisible by $6$. This is false, since $n=4$ breaks it.
- **Inverse:** if $n$ is not divisible by $6$, then $n$ is not even. This is false, and $n=4$ breaks it too.
- **Contrapositive:** if $n$ is odd, then $n$ is not divisible by $6$. This is true, as it must be.

The contrapositive is the only one built by **two** operations, and it is the only one that is safe. The
**converse and the inverse are contrapositives of each other**, so they are true or false **together**.

**A picture.** Read $P\Rightarrow Q$ as "circle $P$ sits inside circle $Q$".

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "P ⇒ Q means every P is a Q. The contrapositive re-reads the same picture; the converse asks for a different one."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
PC, QC, RC, VC = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728', '#7a5195'
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), 2.7, fc=QC, alpha=0.10, ec=QC, lw=2))
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((-0.6, -0.2), 1.35, fc=PC, alpha=0.20, ec=PC, lw=2))
ax.text(-0.6, -0.25, '$P$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=15, color=PC)
ax.text(1.55, 1.75, '$Q$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=15, color=QC)
ax.plot([3.7], [-1.9], 'o', color=RC, ms=10, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('outside $Q$\n$\\Rightarrow$ certainly outside $P$\n(the contrapositive: same picture)',
            (3.7, -1.9), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-70, -52), fontsize=9, color=RC,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=RC, lw=1.2))
ax.plot([1.6], [-0.7], 'o', color=VC, ms=10, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('inside $Q$ but not in $P$\n$\\Rightarrow$ the converse fails here',
            (1.6, -0.7), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(26, 22), fontsize=9, color=VC,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=VC, lw=1.2))
ax.set_xlim(-3.6, 6.2); ax.set_ylim(-4.4, 3.4); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

- **Contrapositive:** outside $Q\Rightarrow$ outside $P$. If all of $P$ is inside $Q$, anything outside $Q$
  certainly missed $P$. It is the same picture read from outside in, which is *why* it is always equivalent.
- **Converse:** inside $Q\Rightarrow$ inside $P$. That would need the two circles to **coincide**, a genuinely
  different claim.

### What an implication actually promises

$P \Rightarrow Q$ makes exactly **one** promise: *you will never find $P$ true while $Q$ is false.*
Everything else is permitted.

**How to read the table.** Each row is one possible situation — a combination of "is $P$ true?" and "is
$Q$ true?". The last column asks: *would that situation make the promise a lie?*

| Row | $P$ | $Q$ | Situation, for "if it rains, the ground gets wet" | Promise broken? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | true | true | it rained, ground wet | no — exactly as promised |
| 2 | true | **false** | it rained, ground **dry** | **YES** — the only way to break it |
| 3 | false | true | no rain, ground wet | no — a burst pipe; the promise said nothing about this |
| 4 | false | false | no rain, ground dry | no — again, nothing was promised |

**Rows 3 and 4 are why the converse and inverse cannot be deduced.** When $P$ is false, the statement
makes **no claim at all** about $Q$ — so $Q$ is free to be either. Row 3 is precisely the counterexample
that kills the converse.

**The same promise, written with "or".** Compare $P \Rightarrow Q$ with "(not $P$) or $Q$" in the same four
rows. An "or" statement is false only when both of its parts are false.

| Row | $P$ | $Q$ | (not $P$) or $Q$ | $P \Rightarrow Q$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | T | T | T | T |
| 2 | T | **F** | **F** | **F** |
| 3 | F | T | T | T |
| 4 | F | F | T | T |

The last two columns are identical, so they say the same thing:

$$P \Rightarrow Q \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\text{not } P) \text{ or } Q.$$

Now read the negation from the table. $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only in row 2, where $P$ is true and $Q$ is
false. So:

$$\text{not}(P \Rightarrow Q) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P \text{ and } (\text{not } Q).$$

The negation of an implication is an "and" statement, not another implication.

**Why this makes the contrapositive equivalent — slowly.**

Two statements are the same statement when they are **broken by exactly the same situations**. So ask,
for the contrapositive "not $Q \Rightarrow$ not $P$", which row breaks *it*.

An implication is broken when its **front is true and its back is false**. For "not $Q \Rightarrow$ not
$P$", that means:

- front true: &nbsp; "not $Q$" is true &nbsp;$\longrightarrow$&nbsp; **$Q$ is false**
- back false: &nbsp; "not $P$" is false &nbsp;$\longrightarrow$&nbsp; **$P$ is true**

So the contrapositive is broken when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false — **row 2, the same single row** that
breaks the original. Same breaking condition, same statement. ∎

Now try the same test on the **converse** ($Q \Rightarrow P$): it is broken when $Q$ is true and $P$ is
false — that is **row 3**, a *different* row. Different breaking condition, different statement. That is
the whole distinction, in one calculation.

**Proving something is false.** To show $P \Rightarrow Q$ is *false*, you must produce a case where $P$
holds and $Q$ fails — a **counterexample**. That is row 2 of the table: not "I disagree", but a specific
situation the statement forbids.

### Why proof by contrapositive works

Because "if $P$ then $Q$" and "if not $Q$ then not $P$" are the same statement, you can prove either one.
Reach for the contrapositive when the **negations are easier to work with than the originals**:

| Original hypothesis | Negation | Which is easier? |
|---|---|---|
| $n^{2}$ is even | $n$ is odd | the **negation** — it gives you $n=2m+1$ |
| $x$ is irrational | $x$ is rational | the **negation** — it gives you $x=p/q$ |
| "at least one of …" | "none of …" | the **negation** — one case instead of many |

For example, to prove "if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even", prove "if $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd" instead.
If $n=2m+1$ for some integer $m$, then

$$n^2=4m^2+4m+1=2\left(2m^2+2m\right)+1 ,$$

which is odd. Attacking the original directly gives only $n^2=2k$, and that is hard to use.

**Not the same as proof by contradiction.** In a proof by contrapositive you assume **not $Q$** and derive
**not $P$**, a clean direct argument. In a proof by contradiction you assume **$P$ and not $Q$ together** and
derive an absurdity. Contradiction is Session 5.

### Do not assume the converse

The commonest error in this topic is to treat "if $P$ then $Q$" as if it also gave "if $Q$ then $P$." It does
not. If a statement **and** its converse are both true, then $P$ and $Q$ are equivalent, an **if and only
if**, which is a stronger claim you must justify separately.

### A 30-second routine for "which is equivalent?"

1. **Name the halves.** Write "$P$ = …, $Q$ = …" on your paper.
2. **Write the theorem as one arrow**, $P \Rightarrow Q$.
3. **Convert each option to an arrow**, using the S1 rules for *if* / *only if*.
4. **Match by shape**, not by meaning:

| What you see | It is | Equivalent? |
|---|---|---|
| $P \Rightarrow Q$ | the original (perhaps restyled) | ✓ |
| not $Q \Rightarrow$ not $P$ | contrapositive | ✓ |
| $Q \Rightarrow P$ | converse | ✗ |
| not $P \Rightarrow$ not $Q$ | inverse | ✗ |

**Never** let the truth of a statement enter this decision. Exam writers deliberately choose theorems
where the converse is *also* true, precisely so that candidates who reason "it's true, so it
must be equivalent" get it wrong.

### Auditing a proof in two lines

Whenever you are asked whether a proof is valid, ignore the algebra at first and write down two things:

$$\textbf{ASSUMED: } \underline{\qquad\qquad} \qquad\qquad \textbf{REQUIRED: } \underline{\qquad\qquad}$$

Then check the match:

| Assumed → concluded | Verdict |
|---|---|
| exactly what was required | ✓ valid (direct proof) |
| **not $Q$** → **not $P$**, when $P \Rightarrow Q$ was required | ✓ valid (proof by contrapositive) |
| $Q$ → $P$, when $P \Rightarrow Q$ was required | ✗ **proved the converse** |
| not $P$ → not $Q$, when $P \Rightarrow Q$ was required | ✗ **proved the inverse** |

**A quick tell:** a genuine proof by contrapositive **contains negations** — it starts from "suppose $n$
is *even*", "suppose $x$ is *rational*". If a student claims contrapositive but their argument has no
negation anywhere, they have almost certainly proved the converse instead.

### The routine, and negating comparisons

**The routine for any awkward wording:**

$$\text{English sentence}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{“if … then …”}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{contrapositive}
\;\longrightarrow\;\text{(translate back if asked)}$$

**Never operate on the original English directly.** Trying to negate an "only if" sentence in place is how
people produce the *inverse* by accident.

**The three styles, side by side.** Recall from S1 that *only if* keeps the order while a bare *if* swaps
it — which is why the last row looks back-to-front and is the one most often got wrong:

| Statement | As an arrow | Contrapositive | …as an arrow |
|---|---|---|---|
| if $P$ then $Q$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | if not $Q$ then not $P$ | $\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ |
| $P$ **only if** $Q$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | not $Q$ **only if** not $P$ | $\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ |
| $P$ **if** $Q$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | not $Q$ **if** not $P$ | $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ |

*Read the last row carefully.* "$P$ if $Q$" has contrapositive $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$, and writing that
back in "if" style puts the **target first**: **not $Q$ if not $P$**. The tempting "not $P$ if not $Q$"
unpacks to $\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ — the **inverse**.

**Negating comparisons** — get these exactly right, because the wrong options are built from these slips:

| Statement | Its negation |
|---|---|
| $x>3$ | $x\le3$ |
| $x\ge3$ | $x<3$ |
| $x=3$ | $x\ne3$ |
| $1<x<4$ | $x\le1$ **or** $x\ge4$ |

The pattern: **negating a strict inequality gives a non-strict one, and vice versa** — the boundary case
always changes sides. And negating a double inequality gives an **or**, never an *and*.

# Part 1 — Concept checks

Two questions, only to confirm the notes have landed. Everything after them is exam standard.

## Question 1

::: {.question}
Assume this statement is **true**:

> *If it rains, then the ground gets wet.*

For each of the following, state whether it **must** be true, **must** be false, or **cannot be
determined**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) If the ground is not wet, then it did not rain. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) If the ground is wet, then it rained. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) If it did not rain, then the ground is not wet. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) It rained and the ground is not wet. **[1]**
:::

Identify each one before you judge it: (a), (b), (c) are the contrapositive, the converse and the
inverse in some order. Only one of them is forced to be true. For (b) and (c), ask the honest question —
[could the ground be wet for some other reason?]{.hl} A burst pipe, a hose, a neighbour washing a car.
Part (d) is different in kind: it is not a rearrangement at all, but a claim that the original statement
is *broken*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — why the contrapositive is equivalent, and the converse is not
:::


Let $A$ = "it rains", $B$ = "the ground gets wet". Given: $A \Rightarrow B$ is true.

**(a) Must be true.** This is the **contrapositive** (not $B \Rightarrow$ not $A$). Dry ground rules out
rain, because rain would have guaranteed wet ground. ✓

**(b) Cannot be determined.** This is the **converse** ($B \Rightarrow A$). Wet ground is consistent with
a burst pipe. The original statement simply says nothing about it — [it might be true in some other
world, but it does not *follow*]{.hl}.

**(c) Cannot be determined.** This is the **inverse** (not $A \Rightarrow$ not $B$). Same reason: no rain
does not mean dry ground, because something else could wet it.

**(d) Must be false.** This says $A$ is true and $B$ is false — which is exactly the one combination
$A \Rightarrow B$ forbids. If it could happen, the original statement would be false.

$\blacksquare$

Notice that (b) and (c) received the same verdict. That is not a coincidence: **the converse and the
inverse are contrapositives of each other**, so they always stand or fall together.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (b) or (c) marked "must be false" | They are not *false* — they are **undetermined**. Nothing in the statement settles them either way. |
| (d) treated as a rearrangement | It is not an implication at all. It is the single case that would make the original **false**. |
:::

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Let $a$ and $b$ be integers. Consider

> **If $a$ and $b$ are both odd, then $ab$ is odd.**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Is the statement true? **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Write its converse, and decide whether the converse is true. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Write its contrapositive. Without doing any new work, say whether it is true and explain
how you know. **[2]**
:::

Part (c) is the point of the question, and it should cost you **no effort at all**: once you have settled
(a), the contrapositive's truth is [already decided, because a statement and its contrapositive are the
same statement]{.hl}. If you find yourself proving (c) from scratch, you have missed the shortcut this
whole session is about.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — judging a statement, its converse and its contrapositive
:::


**(a) True.** If $a = 2m+1$ and $b = 2n+1$ then

$$ab = (2m+1)(2n+1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1 ,$$

which is odd. ✓

**(b) Converse:** *If $ab$ is odd, then $a$ and $b$ are both odd.*

This is also **true**. *(If either factor were even, say $a = 2k$, then $ab = 2kb$ would be even. So an
odd product forces both factors odd.)*

**(c) Contrapositive:** *If $ab$ is **not** odd, then $a$ and $b$ are **not** both odd* — more naturally,
*if $ab$ is even, then at least one of $a$, $b$ is even.*

It is **true**, and [we know this without any work: it is the contrapositive of a true statement, and a
statement and its contrapositive are always equivalent]{.hl}. Since (a) is true, so is (c). ✓

$\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Watch the negation in (c).** The negation of "*$a$ and $b$ are **both** odd*" is **not** "*both are
even*" — it is "*at least one is even*". Negating an "and" flips it to an "or": that is Session 4, but the
trap is here already.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Proving (c) from scratch | Unnecessary. (a) true $\Rightarrow$ (c) true, automatically. That is the whole value of the contrapositive. |
| (c) written as "if $ab$ is even, then $a$ and $b$ are both even" | Over-negated. "not (both odd)" means **at least one** is even, not *both*. |
| Concluding from (b) that converses are usually true | Here both directions happen to hold — because "odd product" and "both factors odd" really are the *same condition*, so the pair forms an "if and only if". That is **unusual**: compare the divisible-by-$6$ example in the Notes, where the converse was false. |
:::

# Part 2 — Medium

## Question 3

::: {.question}
$P$ and $Q$ are statements. For each sentence below, write down its **contrapositive**, in the same
style of English as the original.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $P$ only if $Q$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $P$ if $Q$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Hence explain why the contrapositive of *"$x>3$ only if $x^2>9$"* is *"$x^2 \le 9$ only if
$x \le 3$"*. **[2]**
:::

Do not try to negate an "only if" sentence directly — [convert it to "if … then …" first]{.hl}, take the
contrapositive there, and only then translate back if the question wants that style. Trying to shortcut
this is how people produce the inverse by accident. Recall from S1: *only if* keeps the order, a bare
*if* swaps it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — contrapositives of statements written with "only if"
:::


**(a)** "$P$ only if $Q$" means $P \Rightarrow Q$.

Its contrapositive is $\text{not } Q \Rightarrow \text{not } P$, i.e. *if not $Q$, then not $P$*. Written
back in "only if" style:

> **not $Q$ only if not $P$.**

*(Both are correct answers; the official Notes give exactly this pairing.)*

**(b)** "$P$ if $Q$" means $Q \Rightarrow P$ — the arrow starts at $Q$.

Its contrapositive is $\text{not } P \Rightarrow \text{not } Q$, i.e. *if not $P$, then not $Q$*. Written
back in "if" style — remembering that "$X$ **if** $Y$" means $Y\Rightarrow X$, so the **target** is named
first:

> **not $Q$ if not $P$.**

*Check the order carefully.* The tempting answer, "not $P$ if not $Q$", unpacks to
$\text{not }Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$ — that is the **inverse** of the original, not its contrapositive.
The two differ on the row $P$ true, $Q$ false, where the contrapositive is true and the inverse is false.

**(c)** Take $P$ = "$x>3$" and $Q$ = "$x^2>9$". The given sentence is "$P$ only if $Q$", so by part (a)
its contrapositive is "not $Q$ only if not $P$". Now negate each half:

- not $Q$ is "$x^2 \le 9$" &nbsp; *(the negation of $>$ is $\le$, not $<$)*
- not $P$ is "$x \le 3$"

giving exactly **"$x^2 \le 9$ only if $x \le 3$"**. ✓

$\blacksquare$

*Sanity check that it says something true: if $x^2 \le 9$ then $-3 \le x \le 3$, so certainly $x \le 3$. ✓*

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Negating $x > 3$ to $x < 3$ | The negation of "greater than" is **"less than or equal to"**: $x \le 3$. Forgetting the equality case is a standard TMUA trap. |
| Writing (b)'s contrapositive as "not $P$ if not $Q$" | That reads $\text{not }Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$ — the **inverse**. Since "$X$ if $Y$" means $Y\Rightarrow X$, the contrapositive $\text{not }P\Rightarrow\text{not }Q$ is written **"not $Q$ if not $P$"**. |
:::

# Part 3 — Hard

## Question 4

::: {.question}
$m$ is a positive integer. Consider the theorem

$$\text{If } m^2 \text{ is divisible by } 4, \text{ then } m \text{ is even.} \tag{$*$}$$

Which of the following, **taken individually**, is/are equivalent to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; If $m$ is odd, then $m^2$ is not divisible by $4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; If $m$ is even, then $m^2$ is divisible by $4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $m^2$ is divisible by $4$ only if $m$ is even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** II only &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** III only &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** I and II &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** I and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** II and III &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** I, II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** None
:::

Name the halves and write $(*)$ as an arrow before you read the options — ten seconds spent there saves a
minute of confusion. Then classify each of I, II, III as *original / converse / inverse /
contrapositive*. Be warned that [all three statements happen to be **true**, so truth will not
discriminate between them]{.hl}; the question is which ones say *the same thing* as $(*)$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — sorting several rephrasings at exam speed
:::


Let $P$ = "$m^2$ is divisible by $4$" and $Q$ = "$m$ is even". Then $(*) = P \Rightarrow Q$.

**I.** "If $m$ is odd, then $m^2$ is not divisible by $4$" is $\text{not } Q \Rightarrow \text{not } P$ —
negated **and** reversed. That is the **contrapositive**. **Equivalent.** ✓

**II.** "If $m$ is even, then $m^2$ is divisible by $4$" is $Q \Rightarrow P$ — reversed only. That is the
**converse**. **Not equivalent** — even though, as it happens, it is a true statement. ✗

**III.** "$P$ **only if** $Q$" is $P \Rightarrow Q$ — which is $(*)$ itself, word for word.
**Equivalent.** ✓

**Answer: E (I and III).** $\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Why II is the trap.** It is true, it is *about* the same two facts, and it feels like a restatement. But
$Q \Rightarrow P$ is the converse, and [a converse is a different claim even when it is a true one]{.hl}.
The question asks *"equivalent to"*, not *"also true"*.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Including II because it is true | Truth is not equivalence. Compare the **arrows**, not the truth values. |
| Rejecting I because it "looks different" | It is negated and reversed — the definition of the contrapositive, always equivalent. |
| Missing III because "only if" was unfamiliar | "$P$ only if $Q$" is just $P \Rightarrow Q$ — the original, restyled. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 5

::: {.question}
A student is asked to prove:

> **If $n^3$ is odd, then $n$ is odd.**

The student writes:

> *"Suppose $n$ is odd. Then $n = 2k+1$, so*
> $$n^3 = (2k+1)^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1 = 2\left(4k^3 + 6k^2 + 3k\right) + 1 ,$$
> *which is odd. Hence if $n^3$ is odd, then $n$ is odd."*

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Is the student's algebra correct? **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Is the student's **proof** correct? Explain precisely what has been proved and what was
required. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Write a correct proof of the original statement. **[2]**
:::

Read the student's first line and the last line, and ask what was **assumed** versus what was **required**.
[The algebra can be flawless while the logic is wrong]{.hl} — that combination is exactly what Paper 2's
"find the error" questions are built from, and it is far harder to spot than an arithmetic slip.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — spotting a converse used as though it were a contrapositive
:::


**(a) Yes, the algebra is correct.** $(2k+1)^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1$, and that equals
$2(4k^3+6k^2+3k) + 1$, which is odd. Nothing is wrong with any line of it.

**(b) No, the proof is not correct.** Look at what was assumed and what was concluded:

- The student **assumed** *$n$ is odd* and **derived** *$n^3$ is odd*. That proves
  $$(n \text{ odd}) \Rightarrow (n^3 \text{ odd}) .$$
- The question asked for
  $$(n^3 \text{ odd}) \Rightarrow (n \text{ odd}) .$$

So the student has proved the **converse** of what was required. [The converse is not equivalent to the
original, so nothing about the original has been established]{.hl} — the final sentence ("Hence …") does
not follow.

*It is worth noting that the statement the student proved is perfectly true, and so is the one they were
asked for. But proving one does not prove the other, and that is the error.*

**(c) A correct proof.** Use the **contrapositive**: *if $n$ is even, then $n^3$ is even.*

Suppose $n$ is even, so $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Then

$$n^3 = (2k)^3 = 8k^3 = 2\left(4k^3\right) ,$$

which is even. Since a statement and its contrapositive are equivalent, the original — *if $n^3$ is odd
then $n$ is odd* — is proved. $\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The near-miss.** The student's work is only a small edit away from being right: had they *started* from
"$n$ is even" instead of "$n$ is odd", they would have had exactly the proof in (c). Choosing which
statement to assume is the entire skill here.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| "The proof is fine because the algebra checks out" | Correct algebra proving the **wrong statement** is still a failed proof. Always compare *assumed* with *required*. |
| Fixing it by "reversing the steps" | The steps are not reversible as written. Restart from the contrapositive, as in (c). |
| Calling the student's error a contrapositive | They proved the **converse**. Their argument contains no negations at all — the giveaway. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 4 — Exam bank: mock papers

Three from exam-style mock material, and they are deliberately the **same question** growing harder: a rule
of the form "if $P$ then $Q$" is given, and you must pick the one statement that genuinely follows. The
answer is the **contrapositive** every time — what changes is how much work the negation takes. **★** marks
a question that has already come up on a mock sat here.

::: {.callout-important}
## The two negations these questions live on

$$\lnot(P\ \textbf{and}\ Q)=\lnot P\ \textbf{or}\ \lnot Q\qquad\qquad
\lnot(P\ \textbf{or}\ Q)=\lnot P\ \textbf{and}\ \lnot Q$$

**"and" and "or" swap when you negate.** Every wrong option below is built by forgetting that swap, or by
offering the converse instead. Write the contrapositive out **before** reading the options — otherwise the
options write it for you, badly.
:::

---

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
A locked box has two levers, $A$ and $B$, which can be positioned either left or right at any particular
time. It is known that **if lever $A$ is left or lever $B$ is right, then the box is unlocked.**

Which of the following statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** If the box is unlocked then lever $A$ is left or lever $B$ is right.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** If the box is locked then lever $A$ is left and lever $B$ is right.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** If the box is unlocked then lever $A$ is left and lever $B$ is right.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** If the box is locked then lever $A$ is right or lever $B$ is left.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** If the box is unlocked then lever $A$ is right or lever $B$ is left.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** If the box is locked then lever $A$ is right and lever $B$ is left.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — negate the "or")*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**F.** Name the parts: $P$ = "$A$ left **or** $B$ right", $Q$ = "unlocked". The given fact is
$P\Rightarrow Q$, and the only statement guaranteed to follow is the contrapositive
$\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$.

**Negate $Q$:** "locked". **Negate $P$:** $\lnot(A\text{ left or }B\text{ right})
=(A\text{ not left})\ \textbf{and}\ (B\text{ not right})$, i.e. **$A$ right and $B$ left**. So:

> *If the box is locked, then lever $A$ is right **and** lever $B$ is left.* — option **F**.

**Why each other option fails:**

- **A** is the **converse** $Q\Rightarrow P$ — unlocked tells you nothing, since the box might be unlocked
  for some other reason entirely.
- **C** and **E** also start from "unlocked", so they are converse-shaped too.
- **B** and **D** start correctly from "locked" but botch the negation: **D** keeps the "or" instead of
  swapping it to "and", and **B** negates neither lever.

*Notice that exactly one option gets **both** halves right.* The exam builds the distractors by breaking one
thing at a time — the direction, or the "and"/"or" swap. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q16 &nbsp;★</span>

::: {.question}
A safe has three levers, $A$, $B$ and $C$, each of which can be positioned either left or right at any
particular time. The state of the safe (open or closed) depends only on the positions of these three levers.
It is known that:

> **If lever $A$ is right and (lever $B$ is left or lever $C$ is right), then the safe is open.**

Which one of the following statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** If the safe is open, then lever $A$ is right and either lever $B$ is left or lever $C$ is right.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** If the safe is closed, then lever $A$ is left, and either lever $B$ is right or lever $C$ is left.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** If the safe is closed, then lever $A$ is left, lever $B$ is right and lever $C$ is left.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** If the safe is closed, then either lever $A$ is left, or both lever $B$ is right and lever $C$ is left.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** If lever $A$ is left, or both lever $B$ is right and lever $C$ is left, then the safe is closed.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** If the safe is open, then either lever $A$ is left, or both lever $B$ is right and lever $C$ is left.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — a question already met on a mock; a nested negation)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D.** Let $P$ = "$A$ right **and** ($B$ left **or** $C$ right)" and $Q$ = "the safe is open". All we are told
is $P\Rightarrow Q$ — *nothing more*: we do not know whether $P$ is true, nor whether $Q$ is.

**Build $\lnot P$ in two stages**, outside first:
$$\lnot P=\lnot\Big(A\text{ right}\ \textbf{and}\ \big(B\text{ left or }C\text{ right}\big)\Big)
=\underbrace{A\text{ left}}_{\lnot(A\text{ right})}\ \textbf{or}\
\lnot\big(B\text{ left or }C\text{ right}\big),$$
and the inner negation swaps its own connective:
$$\lnot\big(B\text{ left or }C\text{ right}\big)=B\text{ right}\ \textbf{and}\ C\text{ left}.$$

So $\lnot P$ = "**$A$ is left, or both $B$ is right and $C$ is left**", and the contrapositive reads:

> *If the safe is closed, then either lever $A$ is left, or both lever $B$ is right and lever $C$ is left.*
> — option **D**.

**The other five, and what each one is:**

| | Shape | Why it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | the **converse** — the safe being open tells you nothing |
| **B** | $\lnot Q\Rightarrow(\text{something}\neq\lnot P)$ | "$A$ left **and** …" — the outer "or" was not swapped |
| **C** | $\lnot Q\Rightarrow(\text{something}\neq\lnot P)$ | negates all three levers and joins them with "and" |
| **E** | $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ | the **inverse** — does not follow from $P\Rightarrow Q$ |
| **F** | $Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ | starts from "open", from which nothing can be deduced |

*The whole difficulty is the nesting.* Two connectives means two swaps, and B and C are there precisely for
candidates who perform one and stop. **Write $\lnot P$ out fully before looking at any option.**
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
Let $P$ be the set of prime numbers greater than $3$. Consider the following assertion:

> **All members of $P$ can be represented in the form $6n\pm1$.** &nbsp;&nbsp;$(*)$

Which of the following statements, taken individually, is equivalent to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; A number is **not** a member of $P$ **only if** it can **not** be written in the form $6n\pm1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; A **sufficient** condition for a number to be in $P$ is that it can be written in the form $6n\pm1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **If** a number can **not** be written in the form $6n\pm1$, then it is **not** a member of $P$.

| | I equivalent? | II equivalent? | III equivalent? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **B** | Yes | Yes | No |
| **C** | Yes | No | Yes |
| **D** | Yes | No | No |
| **E** | No | Yes | Yes |
| **F** | No | Yes | No |
| **G** | No | No | Yes |
| **H** | No | No | No |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — three disguises for one implication)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G — No, No, Yes.** Write $(*)$ as an implication first. "All members of $P$ are of the form $6n\pm1$"
means
$$(*)\;:\quad x\in P\;\Rightarrow\;x=6n\pm1 .$$
Now translate each statement into the same notation — *this is Session 1's skill doing Session 2's job.*

- **I.** "$X$ **only if** $Y$" means $X\Rightarrow Y$. Here $X$ = "not in $P$" and $Y$ = "not of the form
  $6n\pm1$", so I says
  $$x\notin P\Rightarrow x\neq6n\pm1,$$
  which is the **inverse** of $(*)$ — equivalent to the *converse*, not to $(*)$. **Not equivalent.**
- **II.** "A sufficient condition for $B$ is $A$" means $A\Rightarrow B$, so II says
  $$x=6n\pm1\Rightarrow x\in P.$$
  That is the **converse**, and plainly false besides: $25=6(4)+1$ is not prime. **Not equivalent.**
- **III.** Directly:
  $$x\neq6n\pm1\Rightarrow x\notin P,$$
  which is exactly $\lnot(\text{conclusion})\Rightarrow\lnot(\text{hypothesis})$ — the
  **contrapositive**. **Equivalent ✓**

**Why I and II are the same mistake wearing different clothes.** The inverse and the converse are
contrapositives *of each other*, so they always stand or fall together. Whenever a question offers you both,
the answer to both is the same — and here it is "no". $\;\blacksquare$

*(For the record $(*)$ is true: any integer is $6n,6n\pm1,6n\pm2$ or $6n+3$, and all but $6n\pm1$ are
divisible by $2$ or $3$, so they cannot be prime beyond $3$. But the question never asks whether $(*)$ is
true — only which statements say the **same thing**.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 5 — Exam bank: real past papers

Converse and contrapositive is a **small** slot. Across the eight papers 2016–2023 it is the named topic of
only seven questions — against twenty-nine for necessary/sufficient. But it is never absent for long, and
when it does appear the mark is usually available with no calculation at all.

Every question below is from a genuine TMUA paper. In Questions 10 and 12 you never need to know what the
statement says, only which options **say the same thing**. [The work is translation before it is
mathematics]{.hl} — convert every option into $\Rightarrow$ form first, then look for options that are secretly
each other.


## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q9 &nbsp;◆</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the statement about a pentagon $P$:

> $(*)$ &nbsp; *If at least one of the interior angles in $P$ is $108^\circ$, then all the interior angles in
> $P$ form an arithmetic sequence.*

Which of the following is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; The statement $(*)$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The contrapositive of $(*)$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The converse of $(*)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — a real TMUA question; the one place I and II cannot separate)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D — III only.**

**Start with the structural fact, before any geometry:** *a statement and its contrapositive are logically
equivalent*, so **I and II always have the same truth value**. That instantly eliminates every option
containing exactly one of them — B, C, F and G are gone before you draw a pentagon.

- **I — false.** The interior angles of a pentagon sum to $540^\circ$. Take
  $100^\circ,102^\circ,108^\circ,110^\circ,120^\circ$: the sum is $540^\circ$ and one angle **is** $108^\circ$,
  but the differences are $2,6,2,10$ — not an arithmetic sequence. So the hypothesis holds and the
  conclusion fails.
- **II — false**, automatically, being equivalent to I.
- **III — true.** The converse reads *"if all the interior angles form an arithmetic sequence, then at least
  one is $108^\circ$."* Write the five angles as $a-2d,\;a-d,\;a,\;a+d,\;a+2d$. They sum to $5a$, and that
  must equal $540^\circ$, so $a=108^\circ$. *The middle term of any arithmetic sequence of five angles is
  forced to be $108^\circ$* — so at least one angle is $108^\circ$, whatever $d$ is. ✓

**The lesson.** A false statement can have a true converse; the two carry no information about each other.
But the contrapositive carries **all** of it. *Knowing that pair rule reduced an eight-option question to
four candidates without any mathematics.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

---


## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
A multiple-choice test question offered the following four options relating to a certain statement:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; The statement is true **if and only if** $x>1$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; The statement is true **if** $x>1$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; The statement is true **if and only if** $x>2$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; The statement is true **if** $x>2$

Given that **exactly one** of these options was correct, which one was it?
:::

You are never told what the statement is — and you do not need to. [Each option is a claim about a
set]{.hl}: about the collection of values of $x$ at which the statement holds. Write that set down and the
question becomes one about containment.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — "if" versus "if and only if", with no mathematical content at all
:::

**D.**

**Translate.** Let $T$ be the set of values of $x$ for which the statement is true.

| option | in English | as a claim about $T$ |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | true **iff** $x>1$ | $T=(1,\infty)$ |
| **B** | true **if** $x>1$ | $(1,\infty)\subseteq T$ |
| **C** | true **iff** $x>2$ | $T=(2,\infty)$ |
| **D** | true **if** $x>2$ | $(2,\infty)\subseteq T$ |

*"If" gives containment in one direction only; "if and only if" pins the set down exactly. An equality is a
much stronger claim than a containment, and a stronger claim drags weaker ones along with it.*

**Use the given.** Exactly one option is correct — so **the correct option must not force any other option
to be correct too**. Test each:

- **A is out.** $T=(1,\infty)$ immediately gives $(1,\infty)\subseteq T$, so B would be correct as well.
  *(It gives D too, since $(2,\infty)\subset(1,\infty)$.)*
- **C is out.** $T=(2,\infty)$ gives $(2,\infty)\subseteq T$, so D would be correct as well.
- **B is out.** If $(1,\infty)\subseteq T$ then, because $(2,\infty)\subset(1,\infty)$, also
  $(2,\infty)\subseteq T$ — so D would be correct as well.
- **D survives.** It forces nothing: take $T=(1.5,\infty)$. Then D holds, A fails, C fails, and B fails
  because $1.2\in(1,\infty)$ but $1.2\notin T$. *Exactly one correct, as required.* ✓

**The lesson.** In a "which one is correct" list, [an option that logically implies another option can
never be the unique answer]{.hl} — you can strike it out before doing any mathematics. Here that argument
disposes of three of the four options and never once needs to know what the statement was.
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

---


## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
Which one of **A**–**F** correctly completes the following statement?

> Given that $a<b$, and $\mathrm{f}(x)>0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$, the trapezium rule produces an
> **overestimate** for $\displaystyle\int_a^b \mathrm{f}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ …

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; … **if** $\mathrm{f}'(x)>0$ and $\mathrm{f}''(x)<0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; … **only if** $\mathrm{f}'(x)>0$ and $\mathrm{f}''(x)<0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; … **if and only if** $\mathrm{f}'(x)>0$ and $\mathrm{f}''(x)<0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; … **if** $\mathrm{f}'(x)<0$ and $\mathrm{f}''(x)>0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** &nbsp; … **only if** $\mathrm{f}'(x)<0$ and $\mathrm{f}''(x)>0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** &nbsp; … **if and only if** $\mathrm{f}'(x)<0$ and $\mathrm{f}''(x)>0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$
:::

There are really only two conditions on offer, each dressed three ways. So do the mathematics once — [the
trapezium rule overestimates exactly when the curve is convex]{.hl} — and then spend the rest of the
question on *if*, *only if* and *if and only if*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — one fact, three wordings; the trap is an over-specified condition
:::

**D.**

### Step 1 — the mathematics, which is one line

The trapezium rule replaces the curve by **chords**. If $\mathrm{f}''>0$ the curve is **convex**, every
chord lies **above** it, and the estimate is an **overestimate**. If $\mathrm{f}''<0$ the curve is concave,
the chords lie below, and it is an underestimate. *The sign of $\mathrm{f}'$ plays no part whatsoever —
which is exactly what the question is testing.*

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

CURVE, CHORD = '#1f77b4', '#d62728'
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 8.2))

def panel(ax, f, a, b, n, title, note, loc):
    x = np.linspace(a, b, 400)
    xk = np.linspace(a, b, n + 1)
    chord = np.interp(x, xk, f(xk))          # the straight-line (trapezium) approximation
    ax.fill_between(x, f(x), chord, color=CHORD, alpha=0.22, lw=0,
                    label='gap between chord and curve')
    ax.plot(x, f(x), color=CURVE, lw=2.4, label='the curve $y=\\mathrm{f}(x)$')
    ax.plot(xk, f(xk), color=CHORD, lw=2.0, marker='o', ms=5.5, label='the chords used')
    for xv in xk:
        ax.plot([xv, xv], [0, f(xv)], color='0.75', lw=0.9, zorder=0)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
    ax.text(0.5, 0.06, note, transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set_ylim(0, None); ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
    ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8.5, loc=loc, framealpha=0.95)

panel(axes[0], lambda x: 1/x, 1, 2, 2,
      "$\\mathrm{f}'<0$, $\\mathrm{f}''>0$  (convex)\nchords sit ABOVE  \u2192  OVERestimate",
      'trapezia $0.70833$   vs   exact $\\ln 2 = 0.69315$', 'upper right')
panel(axes[1], lambda x: np.sqrt(x), 1, 9, 2,
      "$\\mathrm{f}'>0$, $\\mathrm{f}''<0$  (concave)\nchords sit BELOW  \u2192  UNDERestimate",
      'trapezia $16.94427$   vs   exact $52/3 = 17.33333$', 'upper left')

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

So **the condition that matters is $\mathrm{f}''>0$**, and it appears in options D, E and F.

### Step 2 — now read the wording

| option | wording | claim | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **D** | *if* | $\mathrm{f}'<0$ and $\mathrm{f}''>0$ $\Rightarrow$ overestimate | **true** |
| **E** | *only if* | overestimate $\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{f}'<0$ and $\mathrm{f}''>0$ | false |
| **F** | *if and only if* | both directions | false |
| **A** | *if* | $\mathrm{f}'>0$ and $\mathrm{f}''<0$ $\Rightarrow$ overestimate | false |
| **B** | *only if* | overestimate $\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{f}'>0$ and $\mathrm{f}''<0$ | false |
| **C** | *if and only if* | both directions | false |

- **D is true.** Convex is enough on its own, so convex-and-decreasing is certainly enough. *A sufficient
  condition is allowed to ask for more than it needs.*
- **E is false.** It would mean an overestimate can happen **only** when $\mathrm{f}$ is decreasing. Take
  $\mathrm{f}(x)=e^{x}$ on $[0,1]$: it is positive, convex and **increasing**, and two strips give
  $1.75393$ against the exact $e-1=1.71828$ — an overestimate with $\mathrm{f}'>0$. *One counterexample is
  all a "necessary" claim needs to die.*
- **F is false** the moment E is, since it asserts E as one of its halves.
- **A is false**, from the lower picture: concave gives an **under**estimate. B and C carry the same
  condition, so they fail too.

### The lesson

*The condition in the options was deliberately over-specified.* Only $\mathrm{f}''>0$ was doing any work;
$\mathrm{f}'<0$ was dead weight. [When an option bundles the condition you need together with one you do
not, "if" survives the extra baggage and "only if" almost never does]{.hl} — because the extra clause gives
the counterexample away. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q20</span>

::: {.question}
$x$ is a real number and $\mathrm{f}$ is a function.

Given that **exactly one** of the following statements is true, which one is it?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; $x\ge0$ **only if** $\mathrm{f}(x)<0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; $x<0$ **if** $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; $x\ge0$ **only if** $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)<0$ **if** $x<0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$ **only if** $x\ge0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** &nbsp; $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$ **if and only if** $x<0$
:::

This is the last question on the paper and it contains no mathematics at all. Six options, but only four
different statements between them — so [translate every line into an arrow first and look for duplicates]{.hl}. The
phrase *"exactly one is true"* is doing far more work than it appears to.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — spotting contrapositive pairs; "exactly one is true" as an elimination tool
:::

**C.**

### Step 1 — translate

Write $P$ for "$x\ge0$" and $Q$ for "$\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$". Then "$x<0$" is $\lnot P$ and
"$\mathrm{f}(x)<0$" is $\lnot Q$. Remember the two rules: *"$A$ only if $B$" is $A\Rightarrow B$*, and
*"$A$ if $B$" is $B\Rightarrow A$* — the "if" one runs backwards.

| option | in English | as an arrow |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $x\ge0$ only if $\mathrm{f}(x)<0$ | $P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ |
| **B** | $x<0$ if $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$ | $Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ |
| **C** | $x\ge0$ only if $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ |
| **D** | $\mathrm{f}(x)<0$ if $x<0$ | $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ |
| **E** | $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$ only if $x\ge0$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ |
| **F** | $\mathrm{f}(x)\ge0$ iff $x<0$ | $Q\Leftrightarrow\lnot P$ |

### Step 2 — two of these pairs are the same statement twice

- **A and B.** Negate and reverse $P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$: it becomes $\lnot(\lnot Q)\Rightarrow\lnot P$,
  i.e. $Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ — which is **B**. *A and B are contrapositives, so they are logically
  equivalent: always both true or both false.*
- **D and E.** Negate and reverse $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$: it becomes $Q\Rightarrow P$ — which is
  **E**. *Same thing again.*

Now apply the given. **Exactly one** statement is true, so neither pair can contain it — a true member
would drag its partner along and give two. Hence

$$\textbf{A},\ \textbf{B},\ \textbf{D},\ \textbf{E}\ \text{are all false,}$$

and the answer is **C** or **F**. *Four options eliminated, and nothing about $\mathrm{f}$ has been used
yet.*

### Step 3 — F or C

**F is false.** Suppose F held. Take any $x$ with $P$ true, i.e. $x\ge0$. Then $\lnot P$ is false, so by F
$Q$ is false too, i.e. $\mathrm{f}(x)<0$. But "$P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$" is exactly **A** — so F being true
would make A true as well, and we are back to two. *F is out for the same structural reason as the pairs.*

**So C.** It remains only to check C can hold alone — take $\mathrm{f}(x)=1$ for every $x$, so $Q$ is
always true:

| | claim | at $\mathrm{f}\equiv1$ |
|---|---|---|
| **C** | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | $Q$ always true, so **true** ✓ |
| **A** | $P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ | fails at $x=0$ |
| **B** | $Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ | fails at $x=0$ |
| **D** | $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ | fails at $x=-1$ |
| **E** | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | fails at $x=-1$ |
| **F** | $Q\Leftrightarrow\lnot P$ | fails at $x=0$ |

Exactly one true. ✓

### The lesson

Four of the six options were **two** statements wearing four costumes. [Translate, find the contrapositive
pairs, and "exactly one is true" wipes them all out at a stroke]{.hl} — long before you decide anything
about $\mathrm{f}$. *This is the single highest-value habit on the whole page: the converse and the
contrapositive of an option are usually sitting elsewhere in the same list.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

:::

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the equation $2^{x}=mx+c$, where $m$ and $c$ are real constants.

Which of the following statements is/are **true**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; The equation has a negative real solution **only if** $c>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The equation has two distinct real solutions **if** $c>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The equation has two distinct **positive** real solutions **if and only if** $c\le1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

Here the translation is the easy half. [Each statement is a claim about *every* pair $(m,c)$]{.hl}, so each
one dies to a single pair of numbers — and the cheapest numbers are the degenerate ones. Look at what each
statement **fails to mention**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — "only if" / "if" / "iff" applied to a family of curves; counterexample by degenerate choice
:::

**A — none of them.**

The equation asks where the line $y=mx+c$ meets the curve $y=2^{x}$. Note that $c$ is the **$y$-intercept**
of the line and $m$ its gradient; all three statements constrain $c$ and say nothing at all about $m$.
*That omission is the whole question.*

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

CURVE = '#1f77b4'
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 4.6))
x = np.linspace(-3, 2.4, 500)
ax.plot(x, 2.0**x, color=CURVE, lw=2.4, label='$y=2^{x}$')

ax.plot(x, -0.5*x, color='#d62728', lw=1.8, ls='--', label='$y=-x/2$   ($c=0$)')
ax.plot([-1], [0.5], 'o', color='#d62728', ms=8, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('$x=-1$: a negative solution\nwith $c=0\\leq 1$  — kills I',
            (-1, 0.5), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(6, 44), fontsize=9, color='#d62728',
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#d62728', lw=1.1))

ax.axhline(2, color='#2ca02c', lw=1.8, ls='--', label='$y=2$   ($m=0$, $c=2$)')
ax.plot([1], [2], 'o', color='#2ca02c', ms=8, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('$c>1$ but only ONE\nintersection — kills II',
            (1, 2), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-104, 24), fontsize=9, color='#2ca02c',
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#2ca02c', lw=1.1))

ax.axhline(0.25, color='#7a5195', lw=1.8, ls='--', label='$y=1/4$   ($m=0$, $c=1/4$)')
ax.plot([-2], [0.25], 'o', color='#7a5195', ms=8, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('$c\\leq 1$, yet the only root\nis negative — kills III',
            (-2, 0.25), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(6, -46), fontsize=9, color='#7a5195',
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#7a5195', lw=1.1))

ax.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlim(-3, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.25, 5.2)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper left', framealpha=0.95)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### I is false

It claims **negative solution $\Rightarrow c>1$**. Take $m=-\tfrac12$ and $c=0$, so the line is
$y=-\tfrac12x$. At $x=-1$,

$$2^{-1}=\tfrac12 \qquad\text{and}\qquad -\tfrac12\times(-1)=\tfrac12 ,$$

so $x=-1$ **is** a solution — and $c=0$ is not greater than $1$. *A line of negative gradient runs upwards
as $x$ decreases, so it meets the curve somewhere to the left of the $y$-axis no matter how low its
intercept.* The correct wording would have to involve $m$.

### II is false

It claims **$c>1\Rightarrow$ two distinct real solutions**. Take $m=0$ and $c=2$: the equation is $2^{x}=2$,
whose only solution is $x=1$. *A horizontal line meets an increasing exponential exactly once.* Getting two
intersections needs the line to be steep enough to cut the curve twice — again a condition on $m$, which II
never imposes.

### III is false

It claims **two distinct positive solutions $\iff c\le1$**, so it must survive in **both** directions.
The $\Leftarrow$ direction fails at $m=0$, $c=\tfrac14$: then $2^{x}=\tfrac14$ gives $x=-2$ only — one
solution, and a negative one at that. *$c\le1$ on its own forces nothing whatever.*

Since I, II and III are all false, the answer is **A**.

### The lesson

*All three statements constrain $c$ and never mention $m$, yet the number and sign of the intersections
depends on both.* [When a claim about a family of curves names only one of its two parameters, setting the
unmentioned one to zero is usually the fastest counterexample]{.hl} — here $m=0$ alone disposed of II and
III. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

**The whole session in one line:**

> **Reverse only = the converse, and it proves nothing. Negate *and* reverse = the contrapositive,
> and it is free.**

:::
